name: Mark Eden bust developer

lead: The Mark Eden Bust Developer was a clamshell-style spring device sold with an exercise regimen, advertised widely in 1960s and 1970s women's magazines as a way to enlarge and firm the bust. Its appearance payoff was a fuller-looking chest, which exercise can produce through chest and back muscle development.

The ads claimed it transformed flat bustlines into firm, shapely fullness. The US Postal Service ruled in 1966 that the claims were fraudulent, and the product left the market after a 1983 settlement.

paras: Users pressed the spring-loaded device between their hands as resistance exercise, following a routine sold with it. Any change was attributed to enlarged chest and back muscles that could add to bust circumference rather than breast size itself.
No physical harms are documented in the source material. The principal controversy was legal: mail-fraud findings against the advertising and a criminal case against the seller.

angle.text: Buyers used it hoping for a fuller bustline. Chest-muscle exercise can change the contour of the upper torso, but the advertised enlargement of the breasts themselves was the subject of regulatory action [1].

lead: The Mark Eden Bust Developer was a bust-enlargement device and exercise regimen sold by a San Francisco company, heavily advertised in women's magazines in the 1960s and 1970s [1]. Jack and Eileen Feather, California figure-salon entrepreneurs, promoted it, with Playboy centerfold June Wilkinson as a spokeswoman [1].

The regimen used a spring-resistance clamshell device. Ads claimed it turned flat bustlines into firm, shapely fullness, though they rarely showed or described the device [1]. Any measurable effect would have come from enlarging chest and back muscles, which can add to bust circumference without enlarging the breasts [1].
The Postal Service pursued the company over advertising from 1965 and ruled in 1966 that its claims constituted mail fraud [1].
infobox: Mark Eden, San Francisco; Feather company [1]

paras: The company sold the device by mail through magazine advertising and was run by Jack and Eileen Feather, who also marketed Slim Jeans, an Astro-Trimmer and later the Cambridge Diet [1]. The Postal Service began repeated attempts to shut the business down in 1965 and ruled in 1966 that the claims far exceeded puffery, amounting to mail fraud [1].

A consent decree required changes to the advertising language, which the Postal Service later said was violated. In 1970 the company won an injunction against impounding of the device and proceeds, which the Ninth Circuit upheld. Jack Feather was indicted on 11 counts of mail fraud in 1981, and a 1983 settlement, including a $1.1 million fine, ended the product's sales [1].
Nora Ephron wrote about the device in a 1972 Esquire essay, and Lenny Bruce referenced it in his routines. Educators have used its ads as an example of misleading advertising [1].
